lesson.title: Fermentation: Keeping Glycolysis Alive Without Oxygen
lesson.summary: Fermentation is an anaerobic pathway that regenerates NAD+ from the NADH produced by glycolysis, allowing glycolysis and its modest ATP output to continue even when oxygen is unavailable.
lesson.body:
Fermentation solves a very specific problem: glycolysis needs a steady supply of NAD+ to keep oxidizing glucose, but that NAD+ only gets regenerated when NADH hands off its electrons somewhere. Under normal aerobic conditions, that somewhere is the electron transport chain, as covered earlier in this chapter. When oxygen is unavailable, or when a cell simply lacks the machinery to use it, the electron transport chain stalls, NADH piles up, the finite pool of NAD+ runs out, and glycolysis grinds to a halt. Fermentation is the workaround: it regenerates NAD+ by having pyruvate, or a molecule derived from it, accept the electrons from NADH directly, without any membrane, proton gradient, or electron transport chain involved at all.

It is worth being precise about what fermentation is not. It is not a form of anaerobic respiration, and this distinction matters more than the terminology might suggest. Respiration, whether aerobic or anaerobic in the strict microbiological sense, always uses an electron transport chain with some external molecule, oxygen or otherwise, as the final electron acceptor, and always produces additional ATP through oxidative phosphorylation. Fermentation does neither. It produces no additional ATP beyond what glycolysis itself already made through substrate-level phosphorylation, meaning the entire yield of a fermenting cell is capped at that same net 2 ATP per glucose you learned in the very first section of this chapter. Fermentation's only job is regenerating NAD+ so glycolysis can keep running.

The two most well known variants both start from the pyruvate that glycolysis leaves behind, but they dispose of its electrons differently. Alcohol fermentation, used by yeast and some other microorganisms, first removes a carbon from pyruvate as CO2, producing acetaldehyde, and then reduces that acetaldehyde using NADH, producing ethanol and regenerating NAD+ in the process. This is the exact chemistry behind both bread rising, where the CO2 is the useful product, and alcoholic beverages, where the ethanol is. The second variant, lactic acid fermentation, reduces pyruvate directly to lactate without releasing any carbon dioxide, and it is significant enough in human physiology and food science to merit its own detailed treatment next.

From an evolutionary standpoint, fermentation likely represents one of the oldest energy strategies used by life, dating to a time before Earth's atmosphere held significant oxygen. That history connects fermentation directly back to the cellular respiration overview: aerobic respiration should be understood as a later elaboration that was layered on top of the far older core of glycolysis, not as a replacement for it. Even today, fermentation remains indispensable whenever oxygen delivery cannot keep pace with a cell's demand for ATP, whether in an oxygen-poor environment, in tissue temporarily starved of blood flow, or in an organism that has never evolved the machinery for aerobic respiration at all.

The tradeoff fermentation makes is stark but functional: it sacrifices the roughly 30 to 32 ATP per glucose available through full aerobic respiration in exchange for keeping just 2 ATP per glucose flowing, but it keeps that flow going under conditions where aerobic respiration simply cannot operate at all. For a cell facing an immediate oxygen shortage, a small, reliable trickle of ATP is far better than none.
